items.title: 56800_John Simmons oral history interview
items.q: Mary McPartland, and Mary Osborne, they were over there a lot you know.

ctx.x: And they sent the northern soldiers south telling them broke their morale not to speak to the Negros you know and this This put everybody in a fighting mood. So one night, it's like D-Day. Kelley's Stables was on 52nd street between Seventh and Eighth and across the street was the Hickory House. Joseph Marsala

Mary McPartland, and Mary Osborne, they were over there a lot you know. It was -- Red Nova worked over there and the next block with -- which was Sixth Avenue and they renamed it that The Avenue of the Stars, between Sixth and Fifth, but the clubs was mostly about midway to the block and then they ended and then the 21 Club was further up the street. And that entailed the Three Deuces, The Downbeat next door, Tony's was like a supper club, they had a gate under the staircase, I forget this woman's name, Bill…

And all of a sudden in -- it was like D-Day. Everyone emerged into the streets fighting. At the same time. Out of all of the clubs. Don Byas his -- hit somebody in the mouth with his horn; Benny Harris had broke his trumpet across somebody's head. And Teddy Reig, you remember Teddy Reig, big and fat as he has been-- somebody had him down beating the hell out of him, (laughter) a little bitty dude.
